newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian central bank sees capital flight falling.
newsitem.headline: Russian central bank sees capital flight falling.

text.p: Capital flight from Russia will slow down in the next years as economic conditions get better, a senior central bank official said on Monday.
"A fall in capital flight will be connected with an improvement in the economic situation," said Viktor Melnikov, head of the hard currency control and supervision department.
"The central bank's preventive measures allow us to control the most massive means of capital flight," he told a news conference.
Capital flight from Russia amounted to between $60 and $80 billion since the start of economic reforms in 1992.
Official statistics state capital flight at about $50 billion since 1987.
Faked export and import contracts are the main venues of capital flight.

With exports, a contract stating a price lower than the real one is drawn up. The Russian and foreign partners then share the difference. Another way is to put a lower quantity of exported goods in the contract than is actually sold.
With imports, a Russian partner transfers money abroad for goods that are never actually delivered.

The government has stepped up its monitoring of import and export revenue repatriation, for instance with a regulation asking companies to undergo tests on quality, quantity and prices of exported goods.
At home Melnikov said Russians still preferred dollars to roubles, despite falling inflation and the steadier rouble.
He said Russian banks had imported $21 billion in the first eight months of 1996, compared to $20.50 billion in the whole of 1995.
He forecast that imports of dollars would amount to $31 billion this year.
Melnikov said that Russians buy $5 billion a month.
